regions.name: Ovens Murray
regions.blurb: Ovens Murray runs from the Murray River at Wodonga up into the alpine country around Bright, Mount Beauty and Falls Creek. Wodonga and Wangaratta are the main centres, with Beechworth, Rutherglen and the King Valley carrying the wine and tourism trade. Work here is freight along the Hume Freeway, timber, cattle, grape growing and a long winter snow season. It is the Victorian half of the Albury Wodonga cross border market, so most trades quote jobs in both states.

regions.name: Goulburn Valley
regions.blurb: The Goulburn Valley follows the Goulburn River from Lake Eildon north to the Murray at Cobram and Yarrawonga. Shepparton is the centre, surrounded by orchards, dairy farms and fruit processing plants that pull in seasonal workers every summer. Seymour, Nagambie and Euroa sit on the Hume Freeway at the southern end, closer to Melbourne than to Shepparton. Irrigation water decides most of what happens here.

regions.name: Loddon Campaspe
regions.blurb: Loddon Campaspe covers Bendigo, the central goldfields and the Campaspe country north to the Murray at Echuca. Bendigo is the largest inland city in Victoria after Ballarat and runs on health, education, government offices and a growing food sector. Castlemaine and Maldon trade on goldrush streetscapes and a serious arts and maker scene. Echuca and Rochester work off river tourism, dairy and grain.

regions.name: Macedon Ranges
regions.blurb: The Macedon Ranges sit on the Calder Freeway between Melbourne and Bendigo. Kyneton, Woodend and Gisborne are commuter towns with a strong food and wine trade, and Sunbury anchors the southern end where the ranges meet the metropolitan edge. Cool climate vineyards, horse studs and weekend traffic from Melbourne carry a lot of the local spend. Bushfire preparation is a standing job for local trades every spring.

regions.name: Mallee
regions.blurb: The Mallee runs along the Murray from Mildura down through Swan Hill to Kerang, with dry farming country inland. Mildura is the centre for table grapes, citrus, almonds and dried fruit, all of it irrigated from the river. Ouyen and the inland towns run on wheat, barley and sheep. Distances are long, so a trade callout out here often means an hour of driving each way.

regions.name: Wimmera Southern Mallee
regions.blurb: The Wimmera Southern Mallee is broadacre cropping country west of the Grampians. Horsham is the service centre, sitting on the Wimmera River and the Western Highway about halfway between Melbourne and Adelaide. Wheat, barley, lentils and canola set the pace, and the busy months are seeding and harvest. Nhill, Dimboola and Warracknabeal handle grain storage, machinery and freight.

regions.name: Grampians Pyrenees
regions.blurb: Grampians Pyrenees covers the sandstone ranges of Gariwerd and the wine country around Avoca and Great Western. Ararat and Stawell are the main towns, both on the Western Highway. Halls Gap lives on national park visitors, walkers and rock climbers, and empties out in the middle of winter. Sheep, cropping and gold mining fill out the rest of the local economy.

regions.name: Central Highlands
regions.blurb: The Central Highlands centre on Ballarat, a goldrush city of about 116,000 people with a base hospital, a Federation University campus and heavy commuter traffic to Melbourne. Daylesford and Hepburn Springs run on mineral springs, day spas and weekenders. Creswick, Ballan and Bacchus Marsh sit between the two, with Bacchus Marsh growing fast as a Melbourne fringe town. Winters are cold and wet, which keeps heating and roofing trades busy.

regions.name: Barwon
regions.blurb: Barwon covers Geelong, the Bellarine Peninsula, the Surf Coast and the Otway towns down to Apollo Bay. Geelong is the second city of Victoria with about 160,000 people, a deepwater port and a large health and insurance employment base after the Ford plant closed. Torquay, Ocean Grove and Lorne swing hard with the summer season. Colac and the inland towns run on dairy and timber.

regions.name: Great South Coast
regions.blurb: The Great South Coast runs from Camperdown west to the South Australian border, taking in Warrnambool, Port Fairy, Portland and the Hamilton grazing country. Warrnambool is the regional centre with a Deakin University campus and a large dairy processing industry. Portland has the deepwater port, the aluminium smelter and a lot of wind farm work. Inland it is wool, beef and cropping.

regions.name: Latrobe Valley
regions.blurb: The Latrobe Valley is the brown coal and power belt of Victoria, built around Traralgon, Morwell and Moe. Hazelwood closed in 2017 and Yallourn is scheduled to follow, so work has shifted toward health, construction, transmission projects and new energy. Traralgon is the commercial centre and the largest town in Gippsland. Housing is cheap here by Victorian standards and the trade base is deep in industrial skills.

regions.name: South Gippsland
regions.blurb: South Gippsland runs from Warragul and Drouin down through the dairy hills to the coast at Wonthaggi, Inverloch and Phillip Island. Baw Baw Shire is one of the fastest growing parts of regional Victoria, with commuters using the Gippsland line into Melbourne. Dairy, beef and potatoes dominate the farm work, and Wonthaggi services the Bass Coast desalination plant. Population at Cowes and Inverloch roughly doubles over summer.

regions.name: East Gippsland
regions.blurb: East Gippsland stretches from Sale and the Wellington farmland across the Gippsland Lakes to the New South Wales border at Mallacoota. Sale services the offshore Bass Strait oil and gas fields and the RAAF base at East Sale. Bairnsdale and Lakes Entrance are the eastern centres, and Lakes Entrance has the largest fishing fleet in the state. East of Orbost the country turns to forest and the towns get small and far apart.

regions.name: Melbourne Metro
regions.blurb: Melbourne Metro covers the capital and its suburbs, about 5.2 million people spread across roughly 100 kilometres of built up area. Employment runs from the CBD out to the industrial belts at Dandenong, Sunshine and Laverton, and into the growth corridors at Werribee, Melton, Craigieburn and Pakenham. Trades here work by zone rather than by town, and callout fees usually reflect travel across the ring roads. It is the reference market for pricing everywhere else in the state.

regions.name: Mornington Peninsula
regions.blurb: The Mornington Peninsula runs from Mornington south to Portsea and around to Flinders on the Western Port side. Mornington and Rosebud are the main service towns and Sorrento is the expensive end. Holiday houses, wineries, hot springs and boats drive much of the trade work. Demand spikes hard between December and Easter and quiet months follow.

regions.name: Yarra Valley and Dandenong Ranges
regions.blurb: The Yarra Valley and the Dandenong Ranges sit about an hour east of Melbourne. Lilydale is the practical centre and the end of the train line, while Healesville and Yarra Glen carry the wine and tourism trade. Warburton and Yarra Junction run up the valley toward the Upper Yarra reservoir. The hills towns sit in high bushfire risk country, so tree work, gutter clearing and generator installs are regular jobs.

localities.name: Wodonga
localities.blurb: Wodonga is the Victorian half of the Albury Wodonga twin city, split from Albury by the Murray River and the Lincoln Causeway. High Street was rebuilt as Junction Place after the freight line was moved out of the middle of town. Logistics, the Bandiana army base, food manufacturing and health carry the local economy, and most trades here hold licences on both sides of the border.

localities.name: West Wodonga
localities.blurb: West Wodonga sits between Melrose Drive and the Hume Freeway, and holds a lot of the newer housing built since the 1990s. Wodonga TAFE, the Wodonga Plaza end of town and the industrial land off Osburn Street are all close by. It is mostly detached housing on quarter acre blocks, so fencing, decking and split system work are steady jobs.

localities.name: Baranduda
localities.blurb: Baranduda sits under the Baranduda Range about ten minutes south east of Wodonga and has grown fast on new estates. The Leneva Baranduda growth corridor is the main housing release area for Wodonga, so new build trades work here constantly. Baranduda Fields and the primary school are the local hubs, and the range behind the town is a fire risk every summer.

localities.name: Bandiana
localities.blurb: Bandiana is the army logistics base on the eastern edge of Wodonga, home to the Army Museum Bandiana and a large defence workshop and storage precinct. The civilian population is small because most of the land is Commonwealth. Defence contracts and base maintenance work bring trades in from Wodonga and Albury.

localities.name: Bonegilla
localities.blurb: Bonegilla sits between Wodonga and Lake Hume and is best known for Block 19 of the Bonegilla Migrant Experience, the reception centre that processed more than 300,000 post war migrants. Today it is a small rural settlement with lake access at Ludlows Reserve. Holiday houses and the caravan park trade drive most of the local work.

localities.name: Barnawartha
localities.blurb: Barnawartha sits just off the Hume Freeway between Wodonga and Chiltern, with the Ethanol plant and grain handling at Barnawartha North nearby. The old Murray Street shops and the bluestone church give the town its character. Beef, cropping and freight jobs off the freeway are the main employers.

localities.name: Chiltern
localities.blurb: Chiltern kept its 1860s goldrush main street almost intact, which is why film crews keep turning up on Conness Street. Lake Anderson sits at the edge of town and the Chiltern Mount Pilot National Park surrounds it. Heritage building repairs, tourism accommodation and small farm work make up most local trade demand.

localities.name: Rutherglen
localities.blurb: Rutherglen is the fortified wine capital of Australia, with muscat and topaque cellar doors running along the Murray Valley Highway and out towards Wahgunyah. Main Street has the wide verandahs and the Victoria Hotel at its centre. Winery infrastructure, cool rooms, irrigation and tourism accommodation give local trades steady work outside vintage.

localities.name: Wahgunyah
localities.blurb: Wahgunyah sits on the Murray directly opposite Corowa in New South Wales, joined by the John Foord Bridge. The Norske Skog paper mill downstream at Ethel Street was a major employer for decades. River frontage, boat ramps and holiday housing shape the local trade work.

localities.name: Yackandandah
localities.blurb: Yackandandah is a National Trust classified goldmining town about twenty five minutes from Wodonga, with the whole of High Street protected. Totally Renewable Yackandandah has pushed the town towards community solar and battery projects, so local sparkies do a lot of rooftop and storage work. The Yackandandah Folk Festival in March fills every bed in town.

localities.name: Beechworth
localities.blurb: Beechworth has the best preserved gold era granite streetscape in Victoria, centred on Ford Street and Camp Street, including the courthouse where Ned Kelly was committed for trial. Bridge Road Brewers, the Beechworth Bakery and the old asylum site at Mayday Hills draw steady visitor traffic. Heritage overlays cover most of the centre, so builders here deal with permit conditions on almost every job.

localities.name: Tangambalanga
localities.blurb: Tangambalanga sits in the Kiewa Valley about twenty minutes from Wodonga, next door to the Kiewa milk factory that has processed local dairy since the 1930s. The Kiewa Valley Highway runs through and the Murray to Mountains cycling country starts nearby. Dairy sheds, pumps and farm electrical work keep local trades busy.

localities.name: Dederang
localities.blurb: Dederang is a small Kiewa Valley settlement on the road between Wodonga and Mount Beauty, known for its terminal station on the transmission network and its annual picnic races. Grazing and hay dominate the flats along the Kiewa River. Most services come from Yackandandah or Myrtleford.

localities.name: Mount Beauty
localities.blurb: Mount Beauty was built in the 1940s to house workers on the Kiewa Hydroelectric Scheme and still sits under the north face of Mount Bogong, the highest mountain in Victoria. The town is the last stop for supplies before Falls Creek, so winter traffic runs straight through it. Paragliding, mountain biking and the Bogong Alpine Village keep visitors coming in the warmer months.

localities.name: Falls Creek
localities.blurb: Falls Creek is an alpine resort village above Mount Beauty, with lodges built onto the slope and no car access to the village centre during the snow season. Resident population is a few hundred in summer and several thousand in winter. Lodge maintenance, snow clearing, plumbing that survives a freeze and over snow transport are the local trades.

localities.name: Mount Hotham
localities.blurb: Mount Hotham is the highest alpine village in Australia, strung along the Great Alpine Road at about 1750 metres. The airport at Horsehair Plain brings in winter charter flights and the road from Harrietville is chained and closed regularly through the season. Work here is resort maintenance, lodge refits and heating systems that hold up at minus ten.

localities.name: Dinner Plain
localities.blurb: Dinner Plain sits about ten kilometres past Mount Hotham on the Great Alpine Road, built in the 1980s in a timber and stone alpine style with no visible power lines. It is freehold land rather than resort lease, which changes how building and renovation work is approved. Cross country skiing in winter and horse riding in summer bring the visitors.

localities.name: Bright
localities.blurb: Bright sits at the head of the Ovens Valley and fills up twice a year, once for the autumn colours along Gavan Street and again for summer riding on the Murray to Mountains Rail Trail. It is the base for Mount Hotham and Mount Buffalo traffic, and the caravan parks along the Ovens River run near capacity from Boxing Day. Short stay accommodation is a big part of the housing stock, which keeps maintenance and cleaning trades busy year round.

localities.name: Porepunkah
localities.blurb: Porepunkah is five minutes downstream from Bright at the junction of the Ovens and Buckland rivers, and it is where the Mount Buffalo road starts climbing. The airfield here handles gliding and skydiving traffic. Cheaper land than Bright has pulled in new housing along the valley floor.

localities.name: Harrietville
localities.blurb: Harrietville is the last town on the Great Alpine Road before the climb to Mount Hotham, and the chain fitting bay here is where winter traffic stops. Old gold dredge holes sit along the Ovens River and the Bon Accord walking track starts at the edge of town. Accommodation and cafes carry the local economy through the snow season.

localities.name: Myrtleford
localities.blurb: Myrtleford was a tobacco town for most of the twentieth century and the old kilns still stand in paddocks around the valley. Today it runs on hardwood timber processing, hops for the brewing trade, walnuts and chestnuts. Clyde Street is the main strip and the Rail Trail passes straight through the middle of town.

localities.name: Wangaratta
localities.blurb: Wangaratta sits where the Ovens and King rivers meet, on the Hume Freeway and the Melbourne to Albury rail line. Murphy Street and Reid Street form the retail centre, and the town has a base hospital, a large textile history and a growing food manufacturing sector. The Wangaratta Festival of Jazz and Blues each spring is the biggest event on the local calendar.

localities.name: Glenrowan
localities.blurb: Glenrowan is where the Kelly Gang siege ended in June 1880, and the site of the Ann Jones Inn is marked in the middle of town. The Glenrowan wine district around Taminick Gap is known for durif and shiraz. The Hume Freeway bypasses the town, so passing trade depends on the tourist signage.

localities.name: Milawa
localities.blurb: Milawa is the food hub of the King Valley gourmet region, with the Brown Brothers winery, a cheese factory, a mustard maker and an olive grove all within a few kilometres. Weekend traffic from Melbourne is the main visitor flow. Commercial kitchen work, cool rooms and cellar door fitouts are the usual local jobs.

localities.name: Whitfield
localities.blurb: Whitfield sits in the upper King Valley, the centre of the Italian family vineyards that made prosecco a local speciality. The Mansfield Whitfield Road climbs from here over the Powers Lookout country. Vineyard sheds, irrigation and farm machinery repairs are the common jobs.

localities.name: Eldorado
localities.blurb: Eldorado sits between Wangaratta and Beechworth and is best known for the Cocks Eldorado Dredge, the largest of its kind left in the southern hemisphere, sitting in its own flooded pond. The town itself is a handful of streets around the old hotel. Most residents work in Wangaratta or Beechworth.

localities.name: Tallangatta
localities.blurb: Tallangatta was moved eight kilometres west in the 1950s when Lake Hume was enlarged, which is why the town calls itself the town that moved. The 1950s shopfronts along Towong Street are unusually intact for that reason. Dairy, beef and lake tourism drive local work, and the Tallangatta Valley runs east from here toward the Mitta.

localities.name: Corryong
localities.blurb: Corryong is the last Victorian town before the Murray River crossing to Khancoban and the Snowy Mountains, about two hours east of Wodonga. The Man from Snowy River Bush Festival each autumn is the biggest week of the year. Beef, sheep and the health service are the main employers, and the 2020 fires reshaped a lot of the surrounding country.

localities.name: Benalla
localities.blurb: Benalla sits on the Broken River with a lake through the middle of town, the Benalla Art Gallery on its edge and a street art trail that has drawn artists from overseas. Gliding out of Benalla Airport has hosted world championships. Rail freight, light manufacturing and grazing carry the local economy, and the Hume Freeway runs past the eastern edge.

localities.name: Mansfield
localities.blurb: Mansfield is the gateway town for Mount Buller and Lake Eildon, and High Street fills with snow traffic every Friday afternoon in winter. Cattle country surrounds it and the town keeps a working saleyard alongside the cafes. Holiday house maintenance, water tanks and bushfire preparation are constant work for local trades.

localities.name: Mount Buller
localities.blurb: Mount Buller is the closest major snow resort to Melbourne, about three hours by road with the last sixteen kilometres climbing from Mirimbah. The village holds dozens of club lodges and apartment buildings that need pre season certification every year. Summer is mountain biking and the Buller road remains open year round.

localities.name: Bonnie Doon
localities.blurb: Bonnie Doon sits on an arm of Lake Eildon on the Maroondah Highway, with the old rail bridge across the water as its landmark. The lake level swings a long way between wet and dry years, which changes how the caravan parks and boat ramps operate. Holiday houses and camping traffic drive most local demand.

localities.name: Jamieson
localities.blurb: Jamieson sits where the Jamieson River meets the Goulburn arm of Lake Eildon, half an hour south of Mansfield. The Jamieson Brewery and the old courthouse are the visible landmarks in a town of a few hundred people. Four wheel drive touring toward Woods Point and the high country brings the summer trade.

localities.name: Shepparton
localities.blurb: Shepparton is the largest city in the Goulburn Valley and the centre of the fruit and dairy industry, with SPC, Campbells and several large milk processors inside the city limits. Maude Street runs through the retail centre and the painted Moooving Art cows are scattered around town. Roughly one in five residents was born overseas, and the city has long standing Iraqi, Afghan, Albanian and Congolese communities.

localities.name: Mooroopna
localities.blurb: Mooroopna sits across the Goulburn River flats from Shepparton, joined by the causeway on the Midland Highway. The town has its own hospital, McLennan Street shops and a long history in fruit canning. Flood levels on the flats are a live issue for anyone building or insuring here.

localities.name: Tatura
localities.blurb: Tatura is an irrigation town about twenty minutes west of Shepparton, home to a large milk powder plant and the Tatura Irrigation and Wartime Camps Museum. Seven internment and prisoner of war camps operated in the district during the Second World War. Dairy, tomatoes and the SmartFarm research station at Tatura shape the local work.

localities.name: Kyabram
localities.blurb: Kyabram sits between Shepparton and Echuca in heavy dairy country, with the Kyabram Fauna Park on the edge of town. Allan Street is the main shopping strip and the town has its own hospital and district health service. Milk processing, orchards and farm machinery dealerships are the main employers.

localities.name: Numurkah
localities.blurb: Numurkah is on the Goulburn Valley Highway between Shepparton and Cobram, with Melville Street as the main road through town. A large solar farm was built on the edge of town in 2017 and the district runs on dairy and irrigated cropping. The October 2022 flood put water through parts of the town and repair work ran for a long time after.

localities.name: Cobram
localities.blurb: Cobram sits on the Murray opposite Barooga in New South Wales, with Thompsons Beach as the main river swimming spot. It is the centre of a large orchard district for peaches, pears and apples, and packing sheds run hard through summer. Trades here work across the border to Barooga and Tocumwal as a matter of course.

localities.name: Nathalia
localities.blurb: Nathalia sits on Broken Creek at the edge of the Barmah forest, the largest river red gum forest in the world and now a national park. Blake Street is the main strip and the town has a district hospital. Dairy and grazing carry the district, and the forest brings camping and fishing traffic.

localities.name: Yarrawonga
localities.blurb: Yarrawonga sits on Lake Mulwala, formed by the weir on the Murray, and is joined to Mulwala in New South Wales by the bridge at the end of Belmore Street. Retirees and holiday homes have driven heavy residential growth, and the golf club is one of the largest in regional Australia. Boat servicing, air conditioning and new estate work dominate local trade demand.

localities.name: Rushworth
localities.blurb: Rushworth kept its full width goldrush main street, High Street, lined with verandah shopfronts and backed by the Rushworth ironbark forest. Waranga Basin, a large irrigation storage, sits a few kilometres north west and draws campers and skiers. Timber, grazing and a small tourism trade support the town.

localities.name: Euroa
localities.blurb: Euroa sits under the Strathbogie Ranges on Seven Creeks, with Binney Street as the main shopping strip and the 1890 courthouse nearby. The Kelly Gang robbed the National Bank here in 1878. Fine wool, cattle and a growing number of Melbourne buyers on lifestyle blocks shape the district.

localities.name: Violet Town
localities.blurb: Violet Town sits just off the Hume Freeway between Euroa and Benalla, with Honeysuckle Creek running through it. The Saturday market at the recreation reserve is the main gathering point for the district. Grazing and cropping surround the town and most services come from Euroa or Benalla.

localities.name: Nagambie
localities.blurb: Nagambie sits on Lake Nagambie, a widening of the Goulburn River behind Goulburn Weir, and hosts national rowing and water ski events on the straight course. Mitchelton and Tahbilk wineries are minutes away, and Tahbilk has been producing since 1860. Thoroughbred studs around the district add a steady stream of stable and fencing work.

localities.name: Seymour
localities.blurb: Seymour sits on the Goulburn River where the Hume Freeway meets the Goulburn Valley Highway, about ninety minutes from Melbourne by train. Puckapunyal Military Area is fifteen minutes west and is a major local employer. Station Street carries the retail centre, and the town works as a commuter base for people priced out of the Melbourne fringe.

localities.name: Avenel
localities.blurb: Avenel sits on Hughes Creek just off the Hume Freeway, ten minutes north of Seymour. Ned Kelly went to school here as a boy and saved another child from drowning in the creek. New housing estates on the edge of town have brought in commuters using the Seymour rail line.

localities.name: Kilmore
localities.blurb: Kilmore claims to be the oldest inland town in Victoria, settled in 1841, and Sydney Street still has the bluestone buildings to show for it. The town has grown quickly as Melbourne commuters push north along the Northern Highway. Kilmore Racecourse and the surrounding horse properties provide a steady stream of fencing and stable work.

localities.name: Broadford
localities.blurb: Broadford sits on Sunday Creek between Kilmore and Seymour, with the Broadford Motorcycle Complex just outside town hosting national events. It has a station on the Seymour line and has grown on the back of Melbourne commuters. A paper mill operated here for decades and light industry still occupies the site.

localities.name: Yea
localities.blurb: Yea sits at the junction of the Melba and Goulburn Valley highways, an hour and a half from Melbourne, with High Street as the main strip. The Great Victorian Rail Trail starts here and runs 134 kilometres to Mansfield and Tallarook. Beef and dairy country surrounds the town, and the Yea Wetlands sit beside the highway.

localities.name: Alexandra
localities.blurb: Alexandra sits between Lake Eildon and the Cathedral Range, with Grant Street as the main road through town and a timber history that goes back to the 1860s. It is the administrative centre for Murrindindi Shire and has a district hospital. Cattle, timber and Eildon holiday traffic are the local economy.

localities.name: Eildon
localities.blurb: Eildon was built to house workers on the Eildon Dam, which holds the largest water storage in Victoria and supplies irrigation the whole way down the Goulburn. The town sits below the dam wall with the pondage on one side and the lake above. Houseboats, marinas and holiday accommodation carry local trade demand, and the population swings hard with school holidays.

localities.name: Marysville
localities.blurb: Marysville was almost entirely destroyed on Black Saturday in February 2009 and was rebuilt through the following decade, so most of the town is now newer than 2010. Steavenson Falls sits a few minutes out of town and the Lake Mountain snow road starts here. Tourism accommodation and hospitality are the main employers, with Melbourne day trippers arriving through the Black Spur.

localities.name: Bendigo
localities.blurb: Bendigo grew on the richest shallow goldfield in the world and spent the money on buildings, which is why Pall Mall has the Shamrock Hotel, the Law Courts and the Post Office in a row. Today the city runs on Bendigo Health, La Trobe University, government offices and Bendigo Bank, which is headquartered here. The Chinese heritage from the goldfields still shows in the Golden Dragon Museum and the Easter parade.

localities.name: Castlemaine
localities.blurb: Castlemaine has an unusually dense arts and maker population for a town of its size, and the old Castlemaine Woollen Mill and the Mill complex on Walker Street have been converted to studios and food businesses. Mostyn Street is the retail centre and the Botanical Gardens date from 1860. The Castlemaine State Festival runs every second year and fills the district.

localities.name: Maldon
localities.blurb: Maldon was declared Australia's first notable town by the National Trust in 1966, and Main Street has barely changed since the 1860s. The Victorian Goldfields Railway runs steam trains from here to Castlemaine on weekends. Heritage overlays cover nearly the whole town, so renovation work needs planning approval more often than not.

localities.name: Maryborough
localities.blurb: Maryborough is known for its railway station, an enormous 1890 building that Mark Twain described as a railway station with a town attached. High Street carries the retail centre and the town has a long manufacturing history in textiles and food processing. It is the administrative centre for Central Goldfields Shire and has cheaper housing than most of regional Victoria.

localities.name: Heathcote
localities.blurb: Heathcote sits on the Northern Highway between Bendigo and Melbourne, in a shiraz district built on 500 million year old Cambrian soils. High Street is lined with cellar doors and the Heathcote Wine Hub. The town also serves the McIvor Forest and a growing number of lifestyle blocks bought by Melbourne buyers.

localities.name: Echuca
localities.blurb: Echuca has the largest collection of working paddle steamers in the world tied up at the historic Port of Echuca on the Murray. It is joined to Moama in New South Wales by the road bridge, and the two towns function as one economy for retail, trades and tourism. Dairy processing, tomatoes and river tourism are the main employers.

localities.name: Rochester
localities.blurb: Rochester sits on the Campaspe River between Echuca and Bendigo, with a large milk processing plant that is the biggest employer in town. The October 2022 flood inundated the majority of houses and rebuilding work ran for years afterward. Silo art on the edge of town brings the tourist traffic off the Northern Highway.

localities.name: Kyneton
localities.blurb: Kyneton has two main streets, the bluestone shopfronts of Piper Street with its restaurants and antiques, and High Street with the everyday retail. It sits on the Calder Freeway and the Bendigo rail line, about an hour from Melbourne. Kyneton Hospital, the saleyards and a strong food and hospitality trade support local work.

localities.name: Gisborne
localities.blurb: Gisborne sits at the southern end of the Macedon Ranges, forty five minutes from Melbourne on the Calder Freeway, and has grown steadily as a commuter town. Aitken Street is the main strip and the Gisborne Olde Time Market runs on the first Sunday of the month. New estates on the edge of town keep residential builders and landscapers busy.

localities.name: Woodend
localities.blurb: Woodend sits at the foot of Hanging Rock, the volcanic outcrop made famous by the novel and the film. High Street runs along the old Calder route and the town has a station on the Bendigo line. Cool climate wineries, weekend visitors and a growing commuter population drive the local trade.

localities.name: Romsey
localities.blurb: Romsey sits on the Melbourne Lancefield Road on the eastern side of the Macedon Ranges, in grazing and horse country. Main Street has the everyday shops and the town has grown on cheaper land than Gisborne or Woodend. There is no rail line here, so almost everyone drives to Sunbury or Melbourne for work.

localities.name: Sunbury
localities.blurb: Sunbury sits on the Jacksons Creek escarpment at the northern edge of the Melbourne urban area, with electrified trains to the city and the Calder Freeway alongside. Rupertswood Mansion is where the Ashes urn story began in 1882. The town has grown fast, so new estate construction, fencing and pool work are constant.

localities.name: Mildura
localities.blurb: Mildura was laid out by the Chaffey brothers in 1887 around irrigation pumped from the Murray, and the wide grid of Deakin Avenue still follows their plan. Table grapes, dried fruit, citrus, almonds and wine grapes are the backbone of the district, with big seasonal labour demand at harvest. It is closer to Adelaide than to Melbourne, and the Sunraysia Highway and river freight both matter here.

localities.name: Red Cliffs
localities.blurb: Red Cliffs was settled as a soldier settlement block scheme after the First World War and the streets are still laid out on that pattern. Big Lizzie, an enormous 1915 land clearing traction engine, sits in the park in the middle of town. Dried fruit, citrus and a large winery keep the district working.

localities.name: Robinvale
localities.blurb: Robinvale sits on a bend of the Murray opposite Euston in New South Wales, about eighty minutes downstream from Swan Hill. Table grapes, almonds and olives dominate and the town has a large seasonal workforce from the Pacific labour scheme. Housing pressure from that seasonal population is a live local issue.

localities.name: Ouyen
localities.blurb: Ouyen sits at the junction of the Calder and Mallee highways in dry cropping country, an hour south of Mildura. The town is known for its vanilla slice competition and works as the service stop for wheat and sheep properties across the Mallee. Grain handling, machinery repairs and roadhouse trade carry the local economy.

localities.name: Swan Hill
localities.blurb: Swan Hill sits on the Murray where the river turns west, with the Pioneer Settlement open air museum and the Giant Murray Cod statue near the bridge to New South Wales. Campbell Street is the main retail strip. Irrigated horticulture, dairy and a regional hospital are the main employers, and the town serves a large district out to Kerang and Sea Lake.

localities.name: Kerang
localities.blurb: Kerang sits among the Kerang Lakes, a wetland system that holds one of the largest ibis rookeries in the country. Victoria Street is the main road through town on the Murray Valley Highway. Dairy, irrigated cropping and a large tomato growing district around Boort and Cohuna feed local business.

localities.name: Horsham
localities.blurb: Horsham is the largest town in the Wimmera, sitting on the Wimmera River where the Western Highway crosses it, roughly three hours from Melbourne and four from Adelaide. Firebrace Street is the main retail spine and the Horsham Regional Art Gallery holds a strong photography collection. Grain, agricultural research at the Grains Innovation Park, health and freight are the main employers.

localities.name: Nhill
localities.blurb: Nhill sits halfway between Melbourne and Adelaide on the Western Highway, with one of the largest grain silo complexes in the southern hemisphere on its edge. A Karen community from Myanmar settled here from 2010 and now works in the local duck processing plant and manufacturing. The Nhill Aviation Heritage Centre marks the wartime airfield.

localities.name: Dimboola
localities.blurb: Dimboola sits on the Wimmera River with a swimming hole and canoe launch right in the middle of town, and Lake Hindmarsh, the largest freshwater lake in Victoria, is half an hour north. The Little Desert National Park starts just south. Cropping, the rail line and river tourism support local business.

localities.name: Warracknabeal
localities.blurb: Warracknabeal sits on Yarriambiack Creek in the northern Wimmera and is the start of the Silo Art Trail that runs north to Patchewollock. Scott Street has the art deco shopfronts, including the 1938 Warracknabeal Town Hall. Wheat, barley and lentils are the district crops and the town holds a large machinery dealer base.

localities.name: Ararat
localities.blurb: Ararat is the only town in Australia founded by Chinese miners, who struck gold at the Canton Lead in 1857, and the Gum San Chinese Heritage Centre on the Western Highway tells that story. Barkly Street runs through the middle of town. The prison, the health service and wool growing are the main employers, and the Grampians are half an hour west.

localities.name: Stawell
localities.blurb: Stawell hosts the Stawell Gift every Easter, the richest professional footrace in Australia, run on grass at Central Park since 1878. The Stawell gold mine has operated on and off for over 150 years and the site now also houses an underground physics laboratory. Main Street carries the retail centre and the town is the eastern gateway to the Grampians.

localities.name: Halls Gap
localities.blurb: Halls Gap sits in the valley between the Mount William and Wonderland ranges, inside Grampians National Park, and is the base for the Pinnacle and Mackenzie Falls walks. Permanent population is only a few hundred but the town handles hundreds of thousands of visitors a year. Kangaroos on the oval and the caravan parks along Fyans Creek are part of the scenery.

localities.name: St Arnaud
localities.blurb: St Arnaud kept a cast iron verandah streetscape along Napier Street that is among the best preserved in Victoria. It sits at the meeting of the Sunraysia and Wimmera highways in cropping and sheep country. The town has a district hospital and the Kara Kara National Park sits just to the south.

localities.name: Ballarat
localities.blurb: Ballarat grew on the 1850s goldfields and the Eureka Stockade of 1854, and Sturt Street still runs as a wide boulevard with the gardens down the middle. Ballarat Base Hospital, Federation University, Sovereign Hill and a large government office presence are the main employers. It is a cold, wet city by Victorian standards, which shows up in heating, roofing and damp repair work every winter.

localities.name: Wendouree
localities.blurb: Wendouree sits north west of the Ballarat centre and holds the city's main industrial estate along Gillies Street and Norman Street. Lake Wendouree, the rowing course used for the 1956 Olympics, is on its eastern edge. Housing here is mostly post war and 1970s brick, so bathroom and kitchen renovation work is constant.

localities.name: Creswick
localities.blurb: Creswick sits fifteen minutes north of Ballarat and was the birthplace of the Lindsay family of artists, with a gallery in the old town centre. The forestry school here trained generations of foresters and the surrounding plantations still support timber work. The Australian Gold and Wine Trail and the Creswick Woollen Mills draw visitor traffic.

localities.name: Daylesford
localities.blurb: Daylesford sits above Lake Daylesford in the mineral springs country and has built a weekend economy on day spas, restaurants and guesthouses. Vincent Street is the main strip and the Convent Gallery occupies an 1860s building above the town. It has one of the largest same sex couple populations per head in regional Australia and ChillOut Festival each March is the biggest weekend of the year.

localities.name: Hepburn Springs
localities.blurb: Hepburn Springs sits four kilometres north of Daylesford around the Hepburn Mineral Springs Reserve, where the bathhouse has operated since 1895. Swiss and Italian miners settled the area in the 1860s and the old Macaroni Factory still stands nearby. Accommodation and bathhouse maintenance are the main local trade work.

localities.name: Bacchus Marsh
localities.blurb: Bacchus Marsh sits on the Werribee River between Melbourne and Ballarat, with the Avenue of Honour of 281 elms planted in 1918 running into town. Market gardens on the river flats still supply Melbourne, and the town has grown quickly on housing estates at Darley and Maddingley. Trains on the Ballarat line and the Western Freeway make it a heavy commuter town.

localities.name: Geelong
localities.blurb: Geelong is the second largest city in Victoria, built around Corio Bay with the waterfront bollards and Cunningham Pier as its front door. The Ford engine plant and the Alcoa smelter at Point Henry both closed last decade, and the city has shifted into health, education, insurance and the TAC and NDIA head offices. Malop Street and Moorabool Street form the retail core and the port still handles grain, fuel and woodchips.

localities.name: Drysdale
localities.blurb: Drysdale sits in the middle of the Bellarine Peninsula on the road between Geelong and Queenscliff, and has grown fast with new estates on its northern edge. The Bellarine Railway runs heritage trains from the station down to Queenscliff. Wineries and market gardens surround the town, and the Bellarine Rail Trail runs through it.

localities.name: Ocean Grove
localities.blurb: Ocean Grove is the largest town on the Bellarine Peninsula, with a patrolled surf beach and The Terrace as its main shopping street. It has grown heavily with families moving out from Geelong and Melbourne, and the population still climbs sharply over summer. The Ocean Grove Nature Reserve protects one of the last patches of coastal woodland on the peninsula.

localities.name: Barwon Heads
localities.blurb: Barwon Heads sits at the mouth of the Barwon River across the bridge from Ocean Grove, with Thirteenth Beach on the ocean side and the bluff at the river mouth. The town was the filming location for SeaChange and property prices reflect the attention that brought. Holiday houses make up a large share of the housing stock, so maintenance and short stay turnover work is steady.

localities.name: Queenscliff
localities.blurb: Queenscliff sits at the head of Port Phillip opposite Point Nepean, and the ferry to Sorrento runs from the harbour every hour. Fort Queenscliff and the grand hotels along Gellibrand Street date from the 1880s when Melbourne money holidayed here. Fishing, the marine science centre and heritage accommodation carry the local economy.

localities.name: Torquay
localities.blurb: Torquay is where the Great Ocean Road starts and where Rip Curl and Quiksilver were founded, with the surf industry precinct on Baines Crescent still the centre of the trade. Bells Beach is five minutes down the road and hosts the Rip Curl Pro at Easter. The town has grown fast on new estates and is now effectively a southern extension of Geelong.

localities.name: Anglesea
localities.blurb: Anglesea sits where the Anglesea River meets the coast on the Great Ocean Road, with the golf course famous for the kangaroos grazing on its fairways. The Alcoa power station and coal mine here closed in 2015 and the site is being rehabilitated. Holiday houses make up much of the housing stock and the summer population is several times the permanent one.

localities.name: Lorne
localities.blurb: Lorne sits between the Otway forest and Loutit Bay, with Mountjoy Parade running along the front and Erskine Falls in the hills behind. The Pier to Pub swim in January and the Falls Festival at New Year push the town well past capacity. Steep blocks, bushfire overlays and landslip risk make building here more complicated than the postcard suggests.

localities.name: Apollo Bay
localities.blurb: Apollo Bay sits at the base of the Otway Ranges where the Great Ocean Road turns inland toward Lavers Hill. The harbour supports a small commercial fishing fleet working for crayfish and abalone. Great Ocean Walk hikers, the Otway Fly and the Cape Otway lighthouse road bring the visitor traffic, and the town is a long way from any large centre.

localities.name: Colac
localities.blurb: Colac sits on the shore of Lake Colac, the largest natural freshwater lake in Victoria, on the Princes Highway between Geelong and Warrnambool. Murray Street is the main retail strip and the town runs on dairy processing, timber and a large meat works. The Red Rock volcanic complex and the Otway forests are both close by.

localities.name: Warrnambool
localities.blurb: Warrnambool is the main city of the south west coast, with a Deakin University campus, a base hospital and the Warrnambool Cheese and Butter factory at Allansford. Liebig Street is the retail spine and Lady Bay is where southern right whales calve at Logans Beach between June and September. It is the end of the passenger rail line from Melbourne.

localities.name: Port Fairy
localities.blurb: Port Fairy has more than fifty buildings classified by the National Trust, most of them along Sackville Street and Gipps Street, built when this was a whaling and sealing port. The Port Fairy Folk Festival in March fills every bed for eighty kilometres. Fishing, tourism and a growing retiree population support the town.

localities.name: Koroit
localities.blurb: Koroit sits on the rim of the Tower Hill volcanic crater between Warrnambool and Port Fairy, and was settled largely by Irish families whose descendants still farm the district. Commercial Road has the bluestone hotels and the Koroit Irish Festival runs each April. Dairy is the dominant industry around the town.

localities.name: Portland
localities.blurb: Portland was the first permanent European settlement in Victoria, established in 1834, and it still runs on the deepwater port that ships grain, woodchips and livestock. The Portland Aluminium smelter is the largest single employer and a large electricity user. Wind farm construction and maintenance across the district has added a second industrial trade base.

localities.name: Hamilton
localities.blurb: Hamilton calls itself the wool capital of the world and the district still runs merino properties that have been in the same families for generations. Gray Street is the main retail street and the Hamilton Gallery holds a nationally significant decorative arts collection. The base hospital, the abattoir and a large freight yard employ most of the town.

localities.name: Camperdown
localities.blurb: Camperdown sits between the crater lakes of Bullen Merri and Gnotuk on the Princes Highway, with an avenue of elms down Manifold Street and a clock tower at the top. The district is dairy and beef country on rich volcanic soil. The town has a hospital and works as the service centre for the Corangamite shire.

localities.name: Casterton
localities.blurb: Casterton sits on the Glenelg River near the South Australian border and is the birthplace of the kelpie working dog, celebrated with a festival every June long weekend. Sheep and cattle properties surround the town and blue gum plantations have taken over some of the old grazing land. Most specialist services come from Hamilton or Mount Gambier.

localities.name: Traralgon
localities.blurb: Traralgon is the largest town in Gippsland and the commercial centre of the Latrobe Valley, with Franklin Street and the Stockland centre carrying the retail. Australian Paper at Maryvale is the biggest industrial employer in the district. Loy Yang power station sits a few kilometres south and the transmission work around it supports a large electrical trade base.

localities.name: Morwell
localities.blurb: Morwell sits beside the open cut brown coal mine that fed the Hazelwood power station until it closed in 2017, and the town wore the economic hit hard. Government offices, including a large State Revenue Office presence, moved here as part of the transition. Commercial Road is the main strip and housing is among the cheapest in Victoria.

localities.name: Moe
localities.blurb: Moe sits at the western end of the Latrobe Valley on the Princes Freeway, with the Old Gippstown heritage park on its edge and the Baw Baw snowfields road running north from town. The Moe rail station is the main commuter link to Melbourne for the valley. Yallourn power station and the Yallourn open cut are just to the north.

localities.name: Churchill
localities.blurb: Churchill was built in the 1960s as a planned town for power industry workers and later became the home of the Gippsland campus of Federation University. The 30 metre white cigar sculpture beside the highway is the town's best known landmark. Student housing and the surrounding plantation forestry drive most local work.

localities.name: Warragul
localities.blurb: Warragul is the main town of the Baw Baw dairy district, an hour from Melbourne on the Gippsland line, with Queen Street as the retail centre and a regional hospital in town. Growth has been rapid, with new estates spreading north and west and a lot of Melbourne buyers arriving since 2020. Dairy processing, farm services and residential construction are the main sources of work.

localities.name: Drouin
localities.blurb: Drouin sits five minutes west of Warragul on the Princes Freeway and the Gippsland rail line, and the two towns are growing toward each other. The ficifolia trees planted along Princes Way flower red every summer. New housing estates on the northern edge have made this one of the fastest growing towns in regional Victoria.

localities.name: Trafalgar
localities.blurb: Trafalgar sits between Warragul and Moe with the Princes Highway running through and the Blue Rock Lake road heading north from town. Dairy country surrounds it and the local butter factory history is still visible in the older industrial buildings. Commuters use the Trafalgar station on the Gippsland line.

localities.name: Korumburra
localities.blurb: Korumburra started as a black coal town in the 1890s and is now the northern service centre for South Gippsland Shire, on the South Gippsland Highway. Commercial Street runs through the middle and the Coal Creek heritage village sits on the edge of town. Dairy and beef farming dominate the surrounding hills.

localities.name: Leongatha
localities.blurb: Leongatha is the largest town in South Gippsland Shire and the home of a major Saputo dairy processing plant that takes milk from across the district. Bair Street is the main retail strip and the hospital and saleyards serve a wide area. Dairy, beef and the surrounding potato country carry the local economy.

localities.name: Mirboo North
localities.blurb: Mirboo North sits in the Strzelecki Ranges between Leongatha and Morwell, in high rainfall dairy and forest country. Ridgway is the main street and the Grand Ridge Brewery has operated here since the 1980s. A severe storm in February 2024 took out power and trees across the district for weeks.

localities.name: Foster
localities.blurb: Foster is the closest service town to Wilsons Promontory National Park, about half an hour from the park entrance at Yanakie. Main Street has the shops, the Foster War Memorial Arts Centre and the last supermarket before the Prom. Beef and dairy farming fill the surrounding hills and visitor traffic peaks over summer.

localities.name: Wonthaggi
localities.blurb: Wonthaggi was built as a state coal town in 1909 and the State Coal Mine site is still open to visitors. It is now the main service centre for Bass Coast Shire, with a new hospital, and the Victorian desalination plant sits a few kilometres east at Dalyston. Growth from Melbourne retirees and sea changers has pushed steady residential construction.

localities.name: Inverloch
localities.blurb: Inverloch sits at the mouth of Anderson Inlet with a calm bay beach on one side and surf beaches toward Cape Paterson on the other. Dinosaur fossils found in the rock platforms here are some of the most significant in Australia. Coastal erosion along the surf beach has been a live council issue, and the summer population is several times the permanent one.

localities.name: Cowes
localities.blurb: Cowes is the main town on Phillip Island, facing north across Western Port with the jetty at the end of Thompson Avenue. The Penguin Parade at Summerland and the Grand Prix circuit bring millions of visitor nights a year. Holiday houses and short stay accommodation make up much of the housing, so trades here work to a holiday calendar.

localities.name: San Remo
localities.blurb: San Remo sits at the mainland end of the Phillip Island bridge, with the fishing co-op on the jetty where pelicans are fed every afternoon. It is the last stop for supplies before crossing to the island. Commercial fishing, the caravan park and passing traffic on the Phillip Island Road support local business.

localities.name: Sale
localities.blurb: Sale is the onshore base for the Bass Strait oil and gas fields, with Esso and its contractors employing a large share of the local workforce. RAAF Base East Sale trains pilots and air traffic controllers a few kilometres out of town. Raymond Street is the main retail strip and the Port of Sale canal links the town to the Gippsland Lakes.

localities.name: Maffra
localities.blurb: Maffra sits on the Macalister River in the largest irrigation district in southern Victoria, with dairy farms taking water from the Glenmaggie weir. Johnson Street is the main strip and the old sugar beet factory is part of the town's history. It is fifteen minutes from Sale and shares much of its trade base.

localities.name: Yarram
localities.blurb: Yarram sits in the Tarra Valley country between Wilsons Promontory and Ninety Mile Beach, on the South Gippsland Highway. Commercial Road has the shops and the art deco Regent Theatre still runs. Dairy, beef and the timber from the Strzeleckis are the district industries, with Tarra Bulga National Park in the hills behind.

localities.name: Bairnsdale
localities.blurb: Bairnsdale is the administrative centre of East Gippsland Shire and the end of the passenger rail line from Melbourne. Main Street is unusually wide and St Mary's Church at its centre has painted ceilings done by an Italian artist in the 1930s. The hospital, timber, beef and vegetable growing along the Mitchell River flats carry the local economy.

localities.name: Paynesville
localities.blurb: Paynesville sits on the Gippsland Lakes fifteen minutes from Bairnsdale, with canal frontage housing and a free ferry across to Raymond Island where koalas live in the manna gums. Boat maintenance, marina work and holiday house care are the standard trade jobs. The permanent population skews older and grows sharply over summer.

localities.name: Lakes Entrance
localities.blurb: Lakes Entrance is home to the largest commercial fishing fleet in Victoria, working out of the artificial entrance cut through to Bass Strait in 1889. The Esplanade runs along the water with the footbridge across to Ninety Mile Beach. Tourism and fishing carry the town, and summer trade is what pays for the quiet months.

localities.name: Orbost
localities.blurb: Orbost sits on the Snowy River flats where the Princes Highway crosses on the way east to the border. The timber industry that built the town has shrunk sharply since native forest logging ended in Victoria. Dairy and vegetable growing on the river flats continue, and the 2019 and 2020 fires burnt much of the surrounding country.

localities.name: Mallacoota
localities.blurb: Mallacoota is the most easterly town in Victoria, sitting on an inlet twenty three kilometres off the Princes Highway and surrounded by Croajingolong National Park. In the fires of New Year 2020 residents and holidaymakers sheltered on the beach and were evacuated by navy ships. Recovery building work and the summer holiday trade dominate the local economy.

localities.name: Omeo
localities.blurb: Omeo sits high on the Great Alpine Road between Bairnsdale and Mount Hotham, in cattle country that was worked by mountain families for generations. The town holds the Omeo Rodeo and its historic precinct includes the old courthouse and gaol. It is a long way from anywhere, so local trades cover a huge service radius.

localities.name: Melbourne
localities.blurb: Melbourne is the capital of Victoria and the centre of a metropolitan area of about 5.2 million people, laid out on the Hoddle Grid between the Yarra River and Victoria Street. The CBD holds the state government, the courts, the major banks and the universities, with Flinders Street and Southern Cross stations feeding the whole network. Trade pricing set here flows out to the rest of the state, usually with a travel loading attached.

localities.name: Footscray
localities.blurb: Footscray sits five kilometres west of the CBD where the Maribyrnong meets the Yarra, and Barkly Street and Hopkins Street hold the Vietnamese and East African food trade the suburb is known for. Old industrial land along Whitehall Street has been converted to apartments over the past fifteen years. Victoria University has a campus here and the Footscray Market is still the anchor of the shopping strip.

localities.name: Werribee
localities.blurb: Werribee sits between Melbourne and Geelong on the Princes Freeway, with Watton Street as the old main strip and Pacific Werribee as the shopping centre. Werribee Park mansion, the Open Range Zoo and the Western Treatment Plant all sit within the district. Market gardens on the plains still supply a large share of Melbourne's vegetables, and new estates keep pushing west.

localities.name: Dandenong
localities.blurb: Dandenong is the industrial and manufacturing heart of Melbourne's south east, with the South Dandenong industrial estates and the Dandenong South freight precinct alongside the Monash Freeway. Lonsdale Street was rebuilt as a boulevard and the Afghan Bazaar precinct on Thomas Street reflects the local Afghan community. The Dandenong Market has traded on the same site since 1866.

localities.name: Frankston
localities.blurb: Frankston sits at the end of the Frankston rail line where suburban Melbourne meets the Mornington Peninsula, with a long swimming beach and a pier at the end of Wells Street. It is the main service centre for the peninsula, with a hospital, a Monash University campus and Chisholm TAFE. Trades based here typically cover both the south eastern suburbs and the peninsula.

localities.name: Mornington
localities.blurb: Mornington sits on Port Phillip with Main Street running down to the pier and Mothers Beach, and the Wednesday street market taking over the strip each week. It is the commercial centre for the northern peninsula, with a hospital and a large industrial estate at Mornington Industrial Park. Boat storage, holiday houses and an older resident population shape local demand.

localities.name: Rosebud
localities.blurb: Rosebud is the main service town for the southern peninsula, strung along Point Nepean Road with the foreshore camping reserve running for kilometres along the beach. The summer camping grounds have operated on the foreshore since the 1950s and still fill every January. Rosebud Hospital, the shopping centre and a large retiree population support steady year round trade work.

localities.name: Sorrento
localities.blurb: Sorrento sits near the end of the peninsula, with the limestone buildings along Ocean Beach Road built in the 1870s from local stone. The ferry to Queenscliff runs from the pier and the back beach faces open Bass Strait. Property prices here are among the highest in regional Victoria and much of the housing is empty outside summer.

localities.name: Lilydale
localities.blurb: Lilydale is the end of the suburban rail line and the practical service centre for the Yarra Valley, with Main Street carrying the retail and a large quarry on the edge of town that has supplied Melbourne with limestone for a century. Melba Park and the Lilydale to Warburton Rail Trail start here. Trades based in Lilydale usually cover the whole valley and the lower hills.

localities.name: Healesville
localities.blurb: Healesville sits at the eastern end of the Yarra Valley with Nicholson Street as the main strip and Healesville Sanctuary, the native wildlife park, a few minutes out of town. The Black Spur road to Marysville starts here and closes for snow or fallen trees more often than visitors expect. Wineries, tourism accommodation and a large tree change population drive local work.

localities.name: Yarra Glen
localities.blurb: Yarra Glen sits on the flats where the Melba Highway crosses the Yarra, surrounded by some of the best known vineyards in the valley including the district around Dixons Creek. The Yarra Glen Racecourse and the Grand Hotel on Bell Street are the local landmarks. Flooding on the river flats and bushfire risk on the ridges both shape how people build here.

localities.name: Warburton
localities.blurb: Warburton sits in a narrow valley on the Yarra River under Mount Donna Buang, where snow falls most winters within ninety minutes of Melbourne. The Rail Trail from Lilydale ends here and a proposed mountain bike network has been the main local development argument for years. Steep blocks, tall mountain ash and high rainfall make tree work and drainage constant jobs.

localities.name: Belgrave
localities.blurb: Belgrave is the end of the suburban rail line in the Dandenong Ranges and the departure station for Puffing Billy, the 1900 narrow gauge steam railway to Gembrook. The shops along Burwood Highway sit under mountain ash and tree ferns. Every property here is in a designated bushfire prone area, so building work carries construction standards that most Melbourne suburbs never see.
